questions.question: Let $L(t)$ change only by jumps of size one, with state-dependent arrival rates $\lambda(n)$, departure rates $\mu(n)$ and time-average probabilities $p(n)$. Which equation is the level-crossing equation for the level between $n$ and $n+1$?
options: $\lambda(n)\,p(n)=\mu(n)\,p(n)$
$\lambda(n)\,p(n+1)=\mu(n+1)\,p(n)$
$\lambda(n)\,p(n)=\mu(n+1)\,p(n+1)$
$\lambda(n)=\mu(n+1)$

questions.question: A sample path $L(t)$ of a queue changes only by jumps of size one. Which pair of events makes the path cross the level between $n$ and $n+1$ upwards and downwards, respectively?
options: An arrival while $L=n$ goes up; a departure while $L=n+1$ goes down.
An arrival while $L=n+1$ goes up; a departure while $L=n$ goes down.
Any arrival goes up; any departure goes down, whatever the state.
An arrival while $L=n$ goes up; a departure leaving $n+1$ behind goes down.

questions.question: For a queue whose number in system $L(t)$ changes only by jumps of size one, why do up-crossings and down-crossings of the level between $n$ and $n+1$ occur at the same long-run rate?
options: Exponential service times make the departure rate equal to the arrival rate in every state.
Between two up-crossings there must be a down-crossing, so the counts differ by at most one.
Poisson arrivals see time averages, so arrival and departure rates agree in every state.
In steady state the system cannot drift, which forces $\lambda(n)=\mu(n+1)$ for each $n$.

questions.question: Let $D(n,t)$ count departures in $[0,t]$ that leave $n$ jobs behind and $Y(n+1,t)$ be the time spent in state $n+1$ during $[0,t]$. What does $\mu(n+1)=\lim_{t\to\infty}D(n,t)/Y(n+1,t)$ measure?
options: The long-run number of departures leaving $n$ behind per unit of total time.
The number of departures from state $n$ per unit of time spent in state $n$.
The reciprocal $1/\mathbb{E}[S]$ of the mean service time, whatever the state.
The departures leaving $n$ behind per unit of time spent in state $n+1$.

questions.question: In a queue with Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$ and room for at most $K$ jobs, an arrival that finds $K$ jobs is blocked. Why does the level-crossing equation use the entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)$ instead of $\lambda(n)$?
options: A blocked arrival leaves $L(t)$ unchanged, so it does not carry the path across any level.
A blocked arrival crosses the level upwards and immediately back down, adding to both sides.
A blocked arrival waits outside and enters later, so it is counted when it finally joins.
By PASTA, $\lambda^{+}(n)$ is the rate at which Poisson arrivals find $n$ jobs present.

questions.question: In a system with unit jumps the time-average probability of state $3$ is $p(3)=0.1$. The arrival rates are $\lambda(3)=4$ and $\lambda(4)=2$; the departure rates are $\mu(3)=8$ and $\mu(4)=5$. What is $p(4)$?

An $M/M/1$ queue has arrival rate $\lambda=2$ and service rate $\mu=5$ per hour, so the level-crossing equations give $p(n)=(1-\rho)\rho^n$ with $\rho=0.4$. What fraction of time are at least two jobs present, $\mathbb{P}(L\ge2)$?
An $M/M/1$ queue has arrival rate $\lambda=3$ and service rate $\mu=5$ per hour, so $p(0)=0.4$ and $p(1)=0.24$. How many times per hour, in the long run, does $L(t)$ jump from $0$ to $1$?

Jobs arrive deterministically at times $0,4,8,\dots$ at a single server and each needs exactly one time unit of service, so $p(0)=3/4$ and $p(1)=1/4$. What is the state-dependent arrival rate $\lambda(0)$, arrivals in state $0$ per unit time spent in state $0$?

Two machines each fail at rate $1$ per day while working, and one mechanic repairs broken machines one at a time at rate $1$ per day, all times exponential. With $L$ the number of broken machines, what is $p(0)$?

An $M/D/1$ queue has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$ and every service lasts exactly $d$, with $\lambda d<1$. A student writes $\lambda\,p(n)=\tfrac{1}{d}\,p(n+1)$ for all $n$ and concludes that $p(n)$ is geometric. Which assessment is correct?
options: The conclusion holds: every service lasts exactly $d$, so departures occur at rate $1/d$ per unit of time in every busy state.
It fails because the level-crossing equation itself requires exponential service times, which an $M/D/1$ queue does not have.
It fails because arrivals that find the server busy have to be counted with an entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)$ instead of $\lambda$.
The equation holds with $\mu(n+1)$ measured on the sample path, which need not equal $1/d$; the geometric form does not follow.

questions.question: In a system with unit jumps, the balance equation of a state $n\ge1$ reads $(\lambda(n)+\mu(n))p(n)=\lambda(n-1)p(n-1)+\mu(n+1)p(n+1)$. How is it obtained from the level-crossing equations?
options: It is the level-crossing equation of the level $n\mid n+1$ with its terms rearranged.
By combining the equations of the levels $n\mid n+1$ and $n+1\mid n+2$, the two cuts above state $n$.
By combining the equations of the levels $n-1\mid n$ and $n\mid n+1$, the two cuts on either side of state $n$.
It cannot be: balance equations need exponential times, cut equations do not.

questions.question: For an $M/M/1$ queue with $\lambda(n)=\lambda$ and $\mu(n)=\mu$, the level-crossing equations give $p(n)=\rho^n p(0)$ with $\rho=\lambda/\mu$. What happens when $\rho\ge1$?
options: Then $p(n)=(1-\rho)\rho^n$ still holds, now with $p(0)=1-\rho\le0$.
Then $\sum_n\rho^n$ diverges, so only $p(0)=0$ fits and the $p(n)$ cannot sum to one.
Then the equation fails, as up-crossings outnumber down-crossings by more than one.
Then $p(n)$ increases in $n$, but normalisation still gives a positive $p(0)$.

questions.question: Customers arrive as a Poisson process at rate $6$ per hour; one who finds $n$ customers present joins with probability $1/(n+1)$, else leaves. Service is exponential with rate $2$ per hour. What is $p(2)/p(0)$?

A single-server queue has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=1$, exponential services at rate $\mu=2$, and room for at most $2$ jobs in total; arrivals finding $2$ jobs are blocked. What fraction of time is the system full, $p(2)$?

A path of $L(t)$ starts at $0$ and visits, jump by jump, the states $0,1,2,3,2,1,2,1,2$ by time $t$. Let $A(1,t)$ count arrivals in state $1$ and $D(1,t)$ departures leaving $1$ behind. What are $A(1,t)$ and $D(1,t)$?

Jobs arrive in pairs: pair arrivals form a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ and each adds two jobs. One exponential server with rate $\mu$ serves jobs one at a time, the queue is stable, and $n\ge1$. Which equation holds for the level between $n$ and $n+1$?
options: $\lambda\,p(n)=\mu\,p(n+1)$
$2\lambda\,p(n)=\mu\,p(n+1)$
$\lambda\,p(n-1)=\mu\,p(n+1)$

questions.question: In a $G/G/c$ queue with unit jumps, arrival rate $\lambda$ and departure rate $\delta$, level crossing gives $\lambda\pi(n)=\delta\,\delta(n)$, with $\pi(n)$ the fraction of arrivals finding $n$ jobs and $\delta(n)$ the fraction of departures leaving $n$. What reduces this to $\pi(n)=\delta(n)$?
options: Rate stability, so that the departure rate $\delta$ equals the arrival rate $\lambda$.
Poisson arrivals, so that PASTA gives $\pi(n)=p(n)$ for every state $n$.
Exponential service times, so that $\mu(n+1)=\mu$ in every busy state $n+1$.
A single server, so that at most one job can depart at any moment.

questions.question: A stable $M/G/1$ queue has arrival rate $3$ per hour and mean service time $12$ minutes, with an unspecified service-time distribution. What fraction of departing jobs leave the system empty behind them?
options: $0.6$, the fraction of time the server is busy
It cannot be found: departures are not Poisson, so PASTA says nothing about them
$0.4$ only for exponential services; otherwise it needs more than the mean
$0.4$, for any service-time distribution with this mean

questions.question: Single jobs arrive as a Poisson process with rate $2$; at most $3$ jobs fit in the system. The server only serves batches of exactly two jobs, each batch service exponential with rate $1$, so a service moves $2\to0$ or $3\to1$. What is $p(0)$?
